1.

The appellant, by preferring the appeal has called in question to the Judgment of conviction and order of sentences dated 04.03.1995 passed by the learned Assistant Sessions Judge-Cum-Additional Civil Judge (Senior Division), Balasore in S.T. Case No.2 of 1995 arising out of G.R. Case No.296/1994 in connection with Soro P.S. Case No.146/94 in the file of J.M.F.C, Soro.

entities.text: Assistant Sessions Judge-Cum-Additional Civil Judge (Senior Division), Balasore
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: The appellant (accused) has been convicted for commission of offences under Sections 498A and 304B of the IPC, 1860 along with Section 4 of Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.

For the above conviction, the appellant (accused) has been sentenced to undergo R.I. for 3 years and to pay a fine of Rs.5,000/- (rupees five thousands only) in default to undergo R.I. for 30 days for the offence under Section 498A of the IPC, 1860, to undergo R.I. for 10 years for the offence under Section 304B of the IPC, 1860, to undergo R.I. for 6 (six) months and to pay a fine of Rs.1000/- (one thousand only) in default to undergo R.I. for 30 days for the offence under Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 with a direction for running of all the above sentences concurrently.

sentences.text: The case of the prosecution before the trial court was that, accused (appellant) is the husband of the deceased'Sankiri @ Sukantilata'.
Their marriage was solemnized on 15.05.1994 as per the Hindu rites and custom.

At the time of marriage between the accused and the deceased, the brother of the deceased had agreed to give a gold ring to the accused, but after marriage due to some financial difficulties, the brother of the deceased i.e. Khetramohan Das could not able to provide that gold ring to the accused.
For which, the accused and the mother-in-law of the {{ 3 }} deceased started torturing the deceased in her in-laws house.

On 16.07.1994, the elder brother of the accused i.e.
Narayan Sethi informed to the brother of the deceased that, the health condition of the deceased is not well in their house.

So, after hearing about the same, the brother of the deceased along with others came to the house of the accused and found that, the dead body of the deceased has already been cremated by the accused along with his family members.

After knowing about the same, when the brother of the deceased i.e. Khetramohan Das (informant) along with others were returning back from the house of the accused, on their way of return, about 40 to 50 persons including the accused obstructed them and forcibly took their signatures on plain papers and threatened them to kill, in case, they will inform that matter to the police.

So, after the return of the brother of the deceased to his house, he (Khetramohan Das) lodged the F.I.R. vide Ext.2 before the O.I.C. Soro P.S alleging the aforesaid allegations against the accused and his mother.
3. Basing upon such F.I.R., vide Ext.2, the Officer-In-Charge (Umesh Kumar Panda) of Soro Police Station registered Soro P.S. Case No.146 dated 19.07.1994 and he (O.I.C.) himself took up the investigation of the case.

During the investigation, he (I.O, Umesh Kumar Panda) examined the informant, recorded his statements, visited the spot, examined other {{ 4 }} witnesses, seized the articles, released the seized articles of the deceased in the zima of the informant by executing zimanama.

On completion of the investigation, he (I.O) submitted final form, placing the accused along with his father and mother to face trial for the offences under Section 498A and 304B read with Section 34 of the IPC, 1860 and Section 4 of the D.P Act, 1961.

4. Accordingly, after commitment of the case from the court of J.M.F.C., Soro to the court of Sessions Judge, Balasore and on transfer of that case to the court of Assistant Sessions Judge-cum-Additional Civil Judge Senior Division, Balasore, all the three accused persons including the accused (appellant) faced trial in that court having been charged under Section under Section 498A and 304B read with Section 34 of the IPC, 1860 and Section 4 of the D.P Act, 1961.

entities.text: Assistant Sessions Judge-cum-Additional Civil Judge Senior Division, Balasore
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: 5. The plea of the defence was one of complete denial and false implication of the accused persons.

The specific plea/case of the defence as it borne out from the statements of the witnesses of the defence was that, the death of the deceased was not an unnatural death, but her death was natural one by suffering from fits and her dead body was cremated in presence of her parents' family members.
The accused persons are in no way concerned or related with the death of the deceased.

sentences.text: In order to substantiate the aforesaid charges against the accused persons before the trial court, altogether 8 numbers of witnesses were examined on behalf of the prosecution and series of documents were marked as Exhibits from the side of the prosecution, but on the contrary, in support of the above plea of the defence, 3 witnesses were examined on behalf of the defence as D.W.1 to 3.
Out of 8 witnesses of the prosecution, P.Ws.1 and 2 are two brothers of the deceased, P.W.3 is the wife of P.W.2, P.W.4 is the uncle of P.Ws.1 and 2.
Accordingly, P.Ws.1 to 4 are the members of the one family and they (P.Ws.1 to 4) are the parents family members of the deceased.
P.Ws.5 to 7 are the witnesses to the seizure list.
P.W.8 is the sole investigating officer of the case, who had submitted charge sheet against the accused persons on completion of the investigation.

6. After conclusion of hearing and on perusal of the materials and evidence available in the record,
the trial court found the father and mother of the accused (appellant) not guilty for any offences and acquitted them from all the offences/charges, but, whereas the trial court found the accused (appellant) Kailash Sethi (who is the husband of the deceased) guilty for the offences under Sections 498A & 304B of the IPC,1860 and Section 4 of the D.P. Act, 1961 vide Judgment dated 04.03.1995 and passed the order of sentences against him for the aforesaid offences as stated above.
I have already heard from the learned counsel for the appellant (accused) and the learned Standing Counsel for the State.
8. During the course of hearing of the appeal, in order to assail the Judgment of conviction and order of sentences passed by the trial court, the learned counsel for the appellant (accused)

contended that, the Judgment of conviction and order of sentence passed by the trial court against the accused (appellant) for the offences under Sections 498A & 304B of the IPC,1860 and Section 4 of the D.P Act,1961 cannot be sustainable under law.
Because, the said Judgment of conviction has been passed basing upon the evidence of 4 interested witnesses i.e. P.Ws.1 to 4 without any independent corroboration, to their evidence.
For which, the Judgment of conviction and order of sentence passed by the trial court against the accused cannot be sustainable under law.

That too the evidence of P.Ws.1 to 4 are contradictory with each other and their evidence is not making out the offences under Sections 498A/304B of the IPC, 1860 and Section 4 of the D.P. Act, 1961 against the accused.

But on the contrary, learned Standing Counsel for the State argued in support of the Judgment of the trial court by contending that, the well- corroborated evidence of P.Ws.1 to 4 is fully justifying the Judgment of conviction and order of sentences passed by the trial court against the accused for the offences, under Section 498A/304B of the IPC, 1860 and {{ 7 }} Section 4 of Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, which cannot be interfered with.

9. In Para No.18 of the Judgment, the trial court has given observations that, as the accused Kailash Sethi (appellant) had demanded and taken dowry from the brother of the deceased Sankiri, when he Kailash Sethi vs State Of Orissa on 10 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199634937/
3 got marriage to Sankiri and he had tortured Sankiri till her death and as he had not informed the police about the death of his wife Sankiri and as he had not taken his wife to any medical on 16.07.1994, if his wife was seriously ill and as he had also not examined his wife's dead body by any doctor after her death, and as he had cremated the dead body of his deceased wife illegally, for which, the court has got no other alternative, but to presume under Section 113-B of the Indian Evidence Act that, he (accused husband) has caused the dowry death of his deceased wife Sankiri.

entities.text: Kailash Sethi vs State Of Orissa
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: So, prosecution has been able to prove its case under Sections 498A/304B of the IPC, 1860 and Section 4 of the D.P. Act, 1961 against the accused Kailash Sethi(who is the husband of the deceased) as required under law, beyond all reasonable doubts.

In the result, he (accused Kailash Sethi) is found guilty under Sections 498A/304B of the IPC,1860 and Section 4 of the D.P. Act,
1961."

10. It is the settled propositions of law that in order to penalize an accused for an offence under Section 4 of the D.P. Act, 1961, the {{ 8 }} essentials of the Dowry as defined under Section 2 of the said Act are to be fulfilled on behalf of the prosecution.
As per Section 2 of the D.P. Act, 1961, dowry means "any demand or dowry made before, at or after marriage, as a consideration for marriage is called as dowry."

Here in this case at hand, none of the witnesses of the prosecution including the parents family members of the deceased i.e. P.Ws.1 to 4 has deposed a single word in their respective evidence that,
there was any demand by the accused from them through his deceased wife as a consideration of his marriage with the deceased.

For which, due to non- fulfilment of the above essentials of Section-2 of the D.P. Act, 1961 on behalf of the prosecution, offence under Section 4 of the D.P. Act has been failed to be established against the accused (appellant).

11. It is the clarified propositions of law that, general and omnibus nature of evidence relating to the torture on the victim or deceased by her husband or her in laws for non-fulfillment of their any unlawful demand without any specific/definite instances about the particular day, date, time, place and manner of torture shall not make out an offence under Section 498A of the IPC, 1860 against her husband or in laws.

On this aspect the propositions of law has already been clarified by the Hon'ble Court and the Apex court in the ratio of the following decisions:
{{ 9 }}
(i) 1993 Crl. L. J. 3019---Ravindra Pyarelal Bidlan & Others Vs. State of Maharashtra--Para---24---IPC, 1860-Section 498A."
"The entire evidence in this respect is of general allegations.

entities.text: 1993 Crl. L. J. 3019---Ravindra Pyarelal Bidlan & Others Vs. State of Maharashtra--Para---24---IPC, 1860-Section 498A.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: No specific instances of demands and ill-treatment have been given.
General allegations are made against all the accused.
An omnibus statement is made regarding demands, harassment and beating.

So, no reliance can be placed on the said evidence concerning the offence Kailash Sethi vs State Of Orissa on 10 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199634937/
4 under Section 498 A of the IPC, 1860."

entities.text: Kailash Sethi vs State Of Orissa
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: (ii) (2008) 40 OCR---417---Prahallad Budek Vs. State of Orissa- IPC 1860-Section 498A.

entities.text: --Prahallad Budek Vs. State of Orissa- IPC 1860-Section 498A.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "No specific evidence as to when and how demand was made by the appellant for dowry and as to when the deceased was tortured.
The evidence relating to holding of village meetings in that connection is also not specific as to what was decided in such meetings or whether any such decision was ever reduced to writing.

Held,
prosecution failed to establish the charge under Section 498 A IPC, 1860."

(iii) CLT (2008) Supp. Crl. 911---Charia Patra & Bhakta Patra Vs. State of Orissa-IPC, 1860 and Section 498A "Omnibus statement by the witnesses regarding ill-treatment-offence under Section 498 A, IPC is not made out."
(iv) 2016 (1) Crimes 402 (Del.) ---Sonu Kumar & Others Vs. State of Delhi---IPC 1860---Section---498A "Though father, mother and brother in evidence stated deceased was being harassed but no specific instance of harassment was alleged by any one of them.

entities.text: CLT (2008) Supp. Crl. 911---Charia Patra & Bhakta Patra Vs. State of Orissa-IPC, 1860
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: ---Sonu Kumar & Others Vs. State of Delhi
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Prosecution failed to establish that any specific acts of harassment were resorted to by accused to persuade or compel deceased or her relative to meet unlawful demand of property.

So, conviction under Section 498 A of the IPC, 1860 not sustainable"
12.

Here in this case at hand, none of the witnesses of the prosecution including two brothers,
brother's wife and uncle of the decease i.e. P.Ws.1 to 4 has uttered or whispered a single word in their respective {{ 10 }} evidence stating about the specific day, date, time, place and manner of torture on the deceased by the accused (appellant), though they (P.Ws.1 to 4) have deposed in their evidence alleging general allegations that, the accused was subjecting the deceased to torture for non-fulfilment of his demand of a gold ring.

So, by applying the principles of law enunciated in the aforesaid decisions of the Hon'ble Court and apex court to this case at hand, it is held that, prosecution has not become able to make out the offence under Section 498A of the IPC, 1860 against the accused beyond reasonable doubt.

So far as the Judgment of conviction passed under Section 304/B of the IPC, 1860 against the accused is concerned;
Section 304B of the IPC, 1860 provides punishment for dowry death.
There are 3 essentials of Section 304B of the IPC, 1860.

The said essentials are as follows:
"(1) The death of the deceased must have occurred otherwise then under normal circumstances, (2) Her death must have occurred within 7 years of her marriage and (3) The deceased must have been subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or the relatives of her husband soon before her death for or in connection with any Kailash Sethi vs State Of Orissa on 10 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199634937/
5 demand for dowry."
13.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: As per the discussions and observations made in the forgoing paragraphs of this Judgment, it has already been held that, prosecution {{ 11 }} has not become able to establish any torture on the deceased by the accused for non-fulfillment of any demand of dowry.
Therefore, prosecution has not become able to establish the first essential of Section 304B of the IPC, 1860 14.

None of the witnesses of the prosecution including P.Ws.1 to 4 has deposed in their respective evidence that, the accused was subjecting the deceased to cruelty or harassing her soon before her death.

15. As such, prosecution has not also become able to establish first and third essentials of Section 304B of the IPC for making out the offence under Section 304B of the IPC, 1860 against the accused.

16. It is very fundamental in law that, unless and until, all the essentials of Section 304B of the IPC are established, the presumption provided under Section 113 B of the Indian Evidence Act for dowry death shall not become applicable.

So, due to non-proving of all the essentials of Section 304B IPC, 1860 on behalf of the prosecution,
the presumptions for dowry death provided under Section 113B of the Indian Evidence Act has become inapplicable.

Therefore, the observations made by the trial court for holding the accused guilty for the offence under Section 304B of the IPC, 1860 applying the presumptions provided under Section 113 B of the Evidence Act, 1872 has become unsustainable.
17 . That apart, it is the case of the prosecution that, the accused had cremated the dead body of his deceased wife without informing about her death to her parents family members.

The un-assailed testimonies of D.Ws.1 to 3 is clearly going to show that, the dead body of the deceased was cremated after the arrival of the brother of the deceased i.e. the informant (P.W.2).
So, the findings and observations made by the learned trial court in the Judgment that, the accused had cremated the dead body of the deceased without informing her parents family member has also become inacceptable.
On analysis of the facts and circumstances of the case, as per the discussions and observations made above, prosecution has not become able to establish the charges/offences under Section 498A/304B of the IPC, 1860 and Section 4 of the D.P Act, 1961 against the accused beyond reasonable doubt.

sentences.text: For which, there is justification under law for making interference with the Judgment of conviction and order of sentence passed by the learned trial court against the accused through this appeal filed by him accused (appellant).
18. As such, there is merit in the appeal of the appellant.
The same must succeed.
In the result, the appeal filed by the appellant is allowed.

{{ 13 }} The Judgment of conviction and order of sentences dated 04.03.1995 passed by the learned Assistant Sessions Judge-Cum- Additional Civil Judge (Senior Division), Balasore in S.T. Case No.2 of 1995 against the accused (appellant) is set aside.
19. The accused (appellant) is acquitted from the offences/charges under Section under Sections 498A & 304B of the IPC, 1860 and Section 4 of Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.
20. Accordingly, the accused (appellant) is directed to be set at liberty forthwith after being discharged from the bail bonds.
21. Accordingly, the appeal is disposed of finally.
